analysis.title: AI's "Low-Cost Carriers" Are Eating The Frontier Labs Alive; Citadel Securities Says Tokenomics 2.0 Is Here And Margins Are Getting Destroyed
key_insights: Consumption-weighted token prices have fallen about 50% over six months, and average token prices at the frontier have fallen 62%. Citadel attributes this to a growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely from better inference efficiency and competitive pressure.

Open-weight models account for about 65-70% of smart-routing token volume (Vercel AI Gateway data). Citadel says this could pressure excess rents at the frontier as cheaper models become good enough for more enterprise tasks. It cautions that routing-platform users may switch models more readily than the broader customer base.

Ramp data shows essentially no growth in overall enterprise AI spend in Aug and Sept. Citadel attributes this to lower token prices interacting with higher volume. Total spend determines the revenue available to pay for the AI investment cycle.
Ramp data implies 80% of spend on frontier labs comes from 1% of firms. The top 1% spent $9,568 per employee per month in Sept versus $15.7 for the median firm.

Token volumes are up about 5x over six months and about 50% over the last four weeks. Citadel reads this as a substantial demand response to cheaper intelligence. October token volume data implies a further acceleration, but the effect on total spend is unclear.

GPU rental rates point to scarce compute. H100 rentals are up about 14% over six months and 7% over 30 days. B200 rentals are up 27.5% over six months. Strength in older H100s runs against the usual depreciation from obsolescence, which implies sellers of compute can extract rents.

Frontier labs face two pressures at once: lower selling prices and higher compute costs. Using the 27.5% rise in B200 rental rates and a 50% decline in average token prices, throughput must rise 2.55-fold just to preserve gross margin. Citadel says this is illustrative, not an estimate of any lab's margins.

Offsets to the margin squeeze include substantial inference efficiency gains over the past year and multi-year compute contracts. Risks are that easy efficiency gains get exhausted, that new hardware costs more and absorbs some of the benefit, and that efficiency gains also reach open-weight models and trigger another round of price cuts.

Citadel's framing: frontier labs are the established airlines, open-weight models are the low-cost carriers, and hyperscaler infrastructure businesses are the airports with stickier demand and more durable margins from supplying scarce compute.

Citadel sees hyperscalers as potentially the most durable beneficiaries of rising inference demand. It says they can fund capacity and withstand a reassessment of frontier profitability better than leveraged neoclouds. A reassessment of frontier profitability would still be difficult for the whole AI complex, given how much infrastructure investment depends on future spending commitments.

sector_views.rationale: Seen as the potentially most durable beneficiaries of inference demand, with diversified cash flows, strong balance sheets and model-agnostic infrastructure that supplies scarce compute.
Leverage leaves them less able than hyperscalers to withstand a reassessment of frontier profitability.
Falling token prices, rising compute costs and open-weight competition squeeze margins. Citadel questions whether expectations for frontier profitability reflect this.

risk_factors: Open-weight competition could intensify and push token prices lower still.
Inference efficiency gains could stall as the easy improvements are exhausted.
New hardware raises throughput but costs more, absorbing part of the benefit.
A reassessment of frontier profitability on margin or commoditisation concerns would hit the whole AI complex, given infrastructure investment tied to future spending commitments.
Total enterprise AI spend has plateaued, which limits the revenue available to repay the AI investment cycle.
Spending is concentrated, with 1% of firms driving 80% of frontier-lab spend.
Routing-platform data (OpenRouter, Vercel) may overstate switching behavior because users who self-select into these platforms experiment more.

tension_points.bull_case: Inference efficiency gains in the last year have been substantial, compute costs can be locked in through multi-year deals, and token volume growth shows accelerating inference demand.
tension_points.bear_case: Open-weight competition cuts token prices while rising inference demand bids up GPU rental rates. Throughput must rise 2.55-fold just to hold gross margin, and easy efficiency gains may run out.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Inference efficiency progress stalling, or open-source competition intensifying, would confirm the margin pressure. Sustained efficiency gains that offset the price declines and compute cost increases would undercut it.

theme_stances.key_argument: Falling token prices and rising compute costs squeeze frontier margins unless inference efficiency keeps compensating.

theme_stances.evidence: sellers of scarce compute are well placed to extract rents
